newsitem.title: INDIA: India struggling to reach consensus on oil prices.
newsitem.headline: India struggling to reach consensus on oil prices.

text.p: India's oil product prices have become a political hot potato with the ruling centre-left coalition government struggling to reach a consensus on what analysts said on Monday was an inevitable measure.
"It is inevitable. They will have to do it (raise product prices)," said Sanjiv Patni, an oil analyst at W.I. Carr brokerage in Bombay.

India's Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, bowing to pressures in Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 13-party coalition, ruled out a hike in petroleum product prices in near future, newspapers reported earlier on Monday.
"The government will only take a decision after there is a consensus on the issue," the Economic Times newpaper quoted Chidambaram as saying at the World Economic Forum in Davos in Switzerland.
Petroleum Ministry officials have said petroleum product prices must be raised to curtail the burgeoning cost of an oil subsidy programme.

The deficit, which is the amount the government owes India's oil companies for selling petroleum products to Indian consumers below world prices, will reach 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) by the end of the 1996/97 (April-March) fiscal year.
"Sustainablity will be a problem because how long can you go on like this," said Ananta Deb Bhattacharyya, economic adviser in the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
Bhattacharyya said December world crude prices had not come down and in fact the prices of diesel and naphtha were increasing.
He said crude prices had shot up to around $23 a barrel in December from $17.5 in June-July 1996.
"It is a question of political consensus not economic consensus," Bhattacharyya said.
Deve Gowda's communist partners in the governing coalition as well as the right-wing opposition Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) have urged him to resist calls to raise oil prices.
But Chidambaram said the issue of raising prices of petroleum products and financing the burgeoning deficit had become a "major concern for the government".

Jay Dubashi, a member of the BJP's economic wing, said Chidambaram's statement had nothing to do with economics and was "It is a question of timing...The left and the Congress do not want a increase in prices now," Dubashi told Reuters.

Dubashi said with elections due in the northern state of Punjab, and the likelihood of national elections if the coalition were to fall, the government considered it politically unwise to raise prices at this stage.

Dubashi expected the government to raise the product prices in May, after the end of parliament's budget session beginning later this month. The 1997/98 budget is scheduled to be unveiled on February 28.
Deve Gowda said last month the government might resort to borrowing to plug the deficit on the oil pool account.
Bhattacharya said borrowing was a very costly proposition since the fiscal deficit would go up and fuel inflation.
"The government has to do it. It is inevitable," said a finance ministry official who did not want to be identified. It is only a question of the right political timing."
Oil prices in India are controlled by the government. Under an "oil pool account mechanism", the state subsidises the price of imported crude sold to refineries.
The country is expected to run an oil import bill of some $9.6 billion in 1996/97 (April-March), and consume around 81 million tonnes of petroleum products.
India's crude oil production in 1996/97 is expected to fall to 27 million tonnes from around 31 million tonnes in the previous year.
